title: T/F/NI + Vocabulary: Confessions of a Storm Chaser (poziom rejonowy/wojewodzki)

tasks.instruction: Przeczytaj ponizszy tekst. Zdecyduj, ktore zdania (1.1.–1.6.) sa zgodne z trescia tekstu (T – True), ktore sa niezgodne (F – False), a ktore zawieraja informacje niepodane w tekscie (NI – No Information). Nastepnie znajdz w tekscie wyrazy lub wyrazenia, ktore odpowiadaja definicjom podanym w punktach 1.7.–1.11. Wymagana jest calkowita poprawnosc ortograficzna odpowiedzi.
tasks.text:
CONFESSIONS OF A STORM CHASER

People always want to know about the moment of the tornado. What they never ask about is the other ninety-nine hours, which is a shame, because that is what the job actually consists of.

I fell into this on a whim. I was twenty-two, I had a car that was more rust than metal, and a friend from my meteorology course rang me on a Thursday evening in May to say that the models looked interesting over Kansas and did I want to come. I said yes without thinking about it for more than about four seconds. We drove through the night, spent the whole of Friday parked outside a petrol station in a town of six hundred people watching the sky do absolutely nothing, and came home. I have been doing it every spring since.

That first trip taught me the thing that all the films get wrong. In the films, chasers career down dirt tracks with a wall of black cloud filling the rear window and something explodes. In reality the job is gruelling in a very boring way. You drive six hundred kilometres to be in the right county by four in the afternoon. You eat terrible food at strange hours. You spend a great deal of time standing beside a road looking upward and waiting for a storm to make up its mind, and most days it does not, and at seven o'clock you call it a day and start looking for somewhere to sleep. Out of thirty chase days in a season, you might see four tornadoes. In a bad year you see none.

The part that does take skill is deciding where to stand. A supercell is not a shapeless blob; it has a structure, and once you can read that structure you know which part of it is dangerous and which part is merely spectacular. You want to be south and east of the storm, looking into it, with a road behind you that runs in a direction you have already checked on the map. The single most important question is never "how close can I get" but "if this thing turns, where do I go". I have watched people who never thought about the second question, and some of them are not chasing any more.

The other misunderstanding is about why anybody does it. Most people assume it is a thrill-seeking hobby, and there is certainly a rush; I am not going to pretend otherwise. But the chasers I respect are the ones who file reports. When a storm produces a tornado, the warning that goes out to the towns in its path is better if somebody on the ground has confirmed what the radar is only guessing at. Twice I have phoned in a report that made it into a warning, and once, in Oklahoma, we came round a bend and found a family standing in their yard filming a wedge tornado about three kilometres away and clearly delighted with it, and we stopped and persuaded them into their basement. They got underground in the nick of time. Their garage did not survive. That evening did more to keep me coming back than any photograph I have ever taken.

My mother remains sceptical about all of this, and I understand why. What I try to explain to her is that the risk is not evenly spread. The most dangerous part of a chase, by a very long way, is the driving: tired people covering enormous distances on wet roads at night. Nobody makes a film about that.

I have a rule now that I did not have at twenty-two. If I am too tired to explain out loud what the storm is doing, I stop chasing it. There is always another Thursday in May.

items.statement: The narrator's first chase was planned carefully several weeks in advance.
items.explanation: FALSE — The narrator 'fell into this on a whim', agreeing on a Thursday evening 'without thinking about it for more than about four seconds'.

items.statement: According to the narrator, most of a chaser's time is spent without seeing anything happen.
items.explanation: TRUE — 'Out of thirty chase days in a season, you might see four tornadoes. In a bad year you see none.'

items.statement: The narrator's friend from the meteorology course still goes chasing every spring.
items.explanation: NO INFORMATION — The text says the narrator has gone every spring since, but says nothing about what the friend does now.

items.statement: The text explains how chasers work out where to position themselves relative to a storm.
items.explanation: TRUE — 'You want to be south and east of the storm, looking into it, with a road behind you that runs in a direction you have already checked on the map.'

items.statement: The narrator regards the way films portray storm chasing as broadly accurate.
items.explanation: FALSE — 'That first trip taught me the thing that all the films get wrong', and the narrator contrasts the films with a job that is 'gruelling in a very boring way'.

items.statement: The narrator has sold storm footage to television companies.
items.explanation: NO INFORMATION — Photographs and filming are mentioned, but the text never says the narrator has sold any footage.

vocabItems.definition: because of a sudden wish or idea, without a particular reason or plan
to stop what you are doing because you are tired or think you have done enough
at the last possible moment, just before it is too late
having doubts about whether something is true, right or useful
